# THEORYs with `tags` `graphs-and-networks`

*Topics — The twenty-eight kinds of claim this anthology files against — the primary axis of both the practice registry and the reading list, and the same twenty-eight for each (ADR-026). The filing rule is the point: take a domain topic when the claim is ABOUT the domain; a claim merely discovered in one still takes its kind. The axis organizes the record, it does not bound it: content the list cannot place is evidence the list is short (ADR-059).*

**Graphs and networks** — graph-structured data and the models that run on it — node, graph and knowledge-graph embeddings, message passing and graph neural networks, their expressive power and positional encodings, graph transformers, geometric and equivariant GNNs, how they are evaluated, over-smoothing, over-squashing, curvature and rewiring, community structure and partitioning, and language models given graphs.

| [THEORY-083](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-083.md) | A message-passing GNN can distinguish no more graphs than the 1-WL test, and reaches that limit only if its neighbor aggregation is injective on multisets, as a sum followed by an MLP is and a mean or max is not | Xu et al. (2019), [LIT-580](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-580.md) — each message-passing layer refines node labels as one 1-WL iteration can at best, so 1-WL bounds what the network separates. Injective aggregation reaches the bound. Sums of an MLP over a multiset are injective. Means lose counts and maxes lose multiplicities. It is a theorem, and it explains the paper's training-fit ordering and the collapse of mean aggregators to chance on featureless graphs. Morris et al. (2019), LIT-840, proved the same bound independently. | Active |
| [THEORY-130](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-130.md) | Skip-gram node embeddings with negative sampling implicitly factorize a closed-form matrix: DeepWalk the log of the degree-normalized average of the first T random-walk transition powers, shifted by log b, and LINE the same with T = 1 | Qiu et al. (2018), [LIT-824](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-824.md) — apply Levy and Goldberg's SGNS optimum ([THEORY-093](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-093.md)) to a random-walk corpus. As walks lengthen, pair counts converge to stationary-weighted transition powers, so DeepWalk's target is log(vol(G)/T · Σ_{r=1..T} (D⁻¹A)^r D⁻¹) − log b and LINE's is the T = 1 case. A derivation, exact under free dot products, noise ∝ degree and infinitely long walks. It names the target, not what a 128-dimensional embedding trained on finite walks reaches. | Active |
| [THEORY-131](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-131.md) | The steeper learning curves of equivariant interatomic potentials come from the higher body order of their local features, not from equivariance as such | Batatia et al. (2022), [LIT-828](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-828.md) — NequIP ([LIT-832](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-832.md)) found that turning on l ≥ 1 features steepened the log-log learning curve and credited equivariance. MACE re-ran the aspirin experiment: invariant models with body order 2, 3 and 4 have slopes −0.33, −0.51 and −0.64, and at body order 4 adding equivariant features leaves the slope at −0.63 to −0.64 and only shifts the curve. Equivariance is one route to higher body order, and body order is what sets the slope. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-132](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-132.md) | In a message-passing GNN, how much one node's output can depend on another node's input is bounded by the graph between them, so wider layers only rescale the bound, deeper ones trade it for vanishing gradients, and only changing the graph moves it | Topping et al. (2021), [LIT-803](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-803.md), and Di Giovanni et al. (2023), [LIT-823](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-823.md), formalizing Alon and Yahav's over-squashing (2020), [LIT-839](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-839.md). The Jacobian between distant nodes is bounded by powers of the normalized adjacency. It is small across very negatively curved edges and between nodes of high commute time. Width multiplies every sensitivity by the same factor. The bounds are theorems, and their predictions hold on synthetic tasks. On real benchmarks, rewiring gains are mostly a few points or less. | Active |
| [THEORY-133](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-133.md) | Raw Laplacian eigenvector encodings underperform because the network must learn invariance to an arbitrary sign on every eigenvector, and building that invariance into the encoder recovers most of what they carry | Lim et al. (2023), [LIT-818](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-818.md). An eigenvector is defined only up to sign, so k of them have 2^k equally valid forms. On ZINC with a GatedGCN and 8 eigenvectors, the MAE falls step by step as less invariance is left to learn. Random flips leave all 2^k and score 0.198. A per-eigenvector encoder leaves 2 and scores 0.148. SignNet's sign-invariant sum leaves none and scores 0.121. The basis half of the paper's argument, for repeated eigenvalues, is not tested on any graph task. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-134](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-134.md) | Stacked GCN propagation drives node features exponentially toward a subspace that keeps only connected-component membership and degree, at a rate set by the weights' scale against the graph's spectrum | Oono and Suzuki (2019), [LIT-827](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-827.md), extending Li et al. (2018), [LIT-816](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-816.md) — over-smoothing. With largest weight singular value s and spectral factor λ < 1, a ReLU GCN's distance from the subspace is at most (sλ)^l times its start. It is a theorem. What it does not establish is that this is why deep GCNs lose accuracy. On sparse citation graphs the condition sλ < 1 is a sliver, and Rusch et al., [LIT-811](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-811.md), show a deep GCN that avoids over-smoothing and degrades just as much. | Active |
